question: Freedom of expression is among the five fundamental rights. Article 11(1) of the EU Charter on Human Rights states that ‘[e]veryone has the right to freedom of expression (...) and to receive and impart information’.

In the case that became known by the press as ‘Qatargate’, on 22 December 2023 the Belgian judicial authorities ordered a prohibition on all the defendants, including MEP Eva Kaili, and their lawyers ‘having direct or indirect contact, in writing or verbally, with the press for anything relating to this investigation’. In the event of non-compliance with these conditions, ‘the suspect could be put under arrest’.
This order was later cancelled by a decision of the court of appeal. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware of the decision taken by the Belgian judicial authorities?
Is an EU Member State allowed to restrict the freedom of expression of individuals and politicians?
Does it intend to take measures to prevent such blatant human rights violations from happening again in Belgium?
answer: Freedom of expression is protected by Article 11 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights and the Commission is committed to ensuring its respect within the remit of its competences. According to its Article 51(1), the Charter applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law.

The matter at stake, and the decision contested by the Honourable Member in the context of national proceedings does not appear to constitute implementation of EU law, since it does not fall in the ambit of those aspects of criminal law and procedure which are subject to harmonisation at EU level.
The EU acquis on procedural rights for suspects and accused persons (1), and in particular Directive (EU) 2016/343 on the presumption of innocence (2), is limited to certain minimum rules.

It imposes an obligation for public authorities not to refer to suspects or accused persons as being guilty, clarifying that this prohibition should not prevent public authorities from publicly disseminating information on the criminal proceedings only where this is strictly necessary for reasons relating to the criminal investigation.

Directive (EU)2016/343 however does not regulate matters concerning direct or indirect contacts of defendants with the press during ongoing investigations. In such cases, it is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations.

Directive 2010/64/EU on the right to interpretation and translation, Directive 2012/13/EU on the right to information, Directive 2013/48/EU on the right of access to a lawyer, Directive (EU) 2016/343 on the strengthening of certain aspects of the presumption of innocence and of the right to be present at the trial in criminal proceedings, Directive (EU) 2016/1919 on legal aid and Directive (EU)2016/800 on procedural safeguards for children who are suspects or accused persons in criminal proceedings.
